note: Adversarial review complete. Found critical gaps in headless bootstrap and update UX contradiction.

findings.criterion: (2) onboarding brings up a working, secure-by-default instance with zero manual token handling
findings.message: Phase 3's 'One-shot out-of-band token bootstrap' specifies opening the browser exactly once. However, the Phase 3 exposure matrix explicitly supports SSH tunnels and Tailscale, which implies the instance may run on a remote headless server. On a headless machine, attempting to automatically launch a local browser will fail, entirely breaking the zero-manual-token-handling onboarding flow. The plan must account for remote/headless onboarding without violating the zero-manual-token requirement or regressing to manual token copy-pasting.

findings.topic: Manual git surgery on update conflict
findings.criterion: (4) works-on-arrival cross-platform... with no manual git surgery
findings.message: Phase 4 claims the update path requires 'no manual git surgery,' but handles local edits by refusing the update with 'explicit stash/reset instructions.' Asking a collaborator to drop to the CLI, run git stash/reset, retry the update, and then manually reapply their stash over the new release is the definition of manual git surgery. If local edits are possible, either the update orchestrator must handle preservation and restoration automatically, or the 'no manual git surgery' claim is false under these conditions.

findings.criterion: (5) none of this regresses the durability... already has
findings.message: Phase 2's Windows durability contract handles rename contention by retrying for ~1s and then 'fails LOUDLY.' While failing loudly prevents torn writes, throwing an exception and dropping a write (or crashing the agent) simply because Windows Defender or Search locked a file for 1.5 seconds is a severe operational regression for Windows collaborators. The ~1s retry bound is often insufficient against Windows AV scanners, meaning the system's runtime resilience will degrade on NTFS.
